nameStory: Aztec tobacco gets its name from the indigenous peoples of Mexico and Central America who cultivated and used this potent plant in religious ceremonies and traditional medicine long before European contact. The word 'tobacco' itself comes from the Taíno word 'tabaco,' referring to the rolled leaves or the pipe used to smoke them.
description: Aztec tobacco is a compact annual plant from the nightshade family that grows 2-4 feet tall with broad, oval leaves and small tubular flowers. Originally from South American rainforests, this robust tobacco species has thick, somewhat sticky leaves and produces clusters of greenish-yellow flowers at the top of sturdy stems. It's much smaller and bushier than common tobacco, with a more concentrated, stocky appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, oval to heart-shaped leaves up to 8 inches long that feel slightly sticky and fuzzy to the touch, with a strong, acrid smell when crushed

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small tubular flowers about half an inch long, typically greenish-yellow or pale yellow, clustered at the tops of stems in dense groups

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Compact, bushy annual plant reaching 2-4 feet tall with sturdy, upright stems and a dense, stocky appearance

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round capsules that split open to release tiny brown seeds, similar to other nightshade family members

habitat: In New England, Aztec tobacco is extremely rare and typically found only in cultivated gardens or as an occasional escape near historical sites or areas with Native American heritage. When present, it prefers well-drained, fertile soil in sunny locations.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms, producing the first fuzzy, oval leaves on short stems.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and begin flowering in mid to late summer, with greenish-yellow tubular flowers appearing in dense clusters.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, followed by seed capsule formation and plant senescence before first frost.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving no above-ground traces until seeds potentially germinate the following spring.

funFact: Aztec tobacco contains up to nine times more nicotine than regular cigarette tobacco - so much that it was traditionally used to make natural pesticides and could be dangerous to handle without gloves!
confusionNotes: Could be mistaken for other large-leaved garden plants, but the sticky, fuzzy leaves with their distinctive acrid tobacco smell when crushed are unmistakable. The small, greenish-yellow flowers also distinguish it from most ornamental plants.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting Mexican origins, Aztec tobacco actually comes from South American rainforests and was traded northward by indigenous peoples. It's important to note that this plant is extremely potent and potentially toxic - never handle extensively without gloves or attempt to use it.
compareHints: Aztec tobacco is much more compact and stocky than woodland tobacco, which grows 4-5 feet tall with larger white flowers. Unlike jasmine tobacco with its fragrant evening-blooming flowers, Aztec tobacco has small, greenish-yellow blooms with little fragrance. The leaves are also much thicker and stickier than its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Woodland tobacco is much taller and more dramatic than its cousin jasmine tobacco, with longer flower tubes and larger leaves.
Jasmine tobacco is much more delicate and ornamental than its cousin woodland tobacco, which grows much taller (up to 10 feet) with smaller white flowers.
